title: Cooper v. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (1984)
summary: An adverse class judgment concerning a general pattern of discrimination did not automatically defeat every class member’s individual claim.
notes:
This case supplies preclusion material within the assigned class-action chapter. It does not expand the syllabus into a complete treatment of the later preclusion chapter.

The class suit was originally an EEOC action (filed March 1977) in which Cooper and three other employees intervened and won certification of a class of Black employees; the district court found a pattern of discrimination only in pay grades 4 and 5, and the Baxter plaintiffs (who had received notice and not opted out) then filed separate individual promotion claims.

Justice Stevens wrote for a unanimous Court: a class judgment on a pattern-or-practice claim precludes relitigation of whether the employer engaged in a pattern of discrimination, but does not bar individual class members from proving discrete individual claims in later suits.

sections.Parties: Employees who had belonged to a discrimination class sought to bring individual claims against the Federal Reserve Bank after the class litigation.
sections.Material Facts: The earlier case challenged general employment policies and practices at the bank’s Charlotte branch. The class received notice and an opportunity for exclusion. Some later individual plaintiffs testified in that proceeding. The litigation addressed a general pattern and certain named individuals’ claims, but did not determine the merits of every class member’s particular promotion decision.
sections.Procedural History: The Fourth Circuit treated the class judgment as precluding the later individual actions. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded.
sections.Issue: Did rejection of the class-wide pattern-or-practice claim bar the separate individual discrimination claims?
sections.Holding: No. The class determination was binding within its scope, but did not itself resolve the distinct individual claims.
sections.Reasoning: A general pattern and an individual discriminatory decision are different issues. An employer can lack a pervasive discriminatory policy yet discriminate in a particular instance. The class judgment prevented another attempt to establish the same general pattern for the period and could have evidentiary significance, but did not decide every employee’s individual experience. Treating it as doing so would pressure every class member to intervene and litigate individually, undermining the representative device’s function.

learning.why: An adverse class judgment concerning a general pattern of discrimination did not automatically defeat every class member’s individual claim.

topics.cp-class-preclusion: Loss of the class-wide pattern claim did not necessarily adjudicate individual discrimination claims.
topics.cp-issue-preclusion: The determination about the employer’s general pattern remained binding even though distinct individual claims survived.
topics.cp-commonality: An individual violation and a companywide pattern require different proof.
topics.cp-finality: The case defines how far a class judgment's claim-preclusive effect reaches into later individual suits.
topics.cp-class-actions: It is a core case on the binding effect of Rule 23 pattern-or-practice litigation on absent members.

mnemonic.rationale: A class win that did not end individual claims
